C. Points to be noted under Master Circular Chapter VII-A:
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

1. Since the new circular is effective for compliance period ending on after June 30, 2020, the
companies which are non-compliant prior to this period and continue to be non-compliant post
June 30, 2020 shall trigger fines and subsequent actions as per SEBI SOP circular dated January
2. Fines would be imposed even during suspension period for non-compliance of regulation 13(1).
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

LODR) would also be included.
4. The review for the submission status of Annual Report (Regulation 34) for the period ended
March 2020, will be done as per provisions of SEBI SOP Master circular.
5. For submission and levy of fine, if the last day of submission and/or next day of submission for
levying fine on the non-compliant Company is on a holiday (including Saturday) then the next
working day shall be considered as the last day of submission and start of levying of fine. The
same would be applicable at the time of review, day of transfer to Z group, issuing reminder to
promoters before freezing, giving intimation for freezing of promoter holding and suspension
date. (Non-working day benefit).
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

6. Freezing of promoter holdings will be done based on the PAN provided by companies while filing

the bifurcation of promoter and promoter group is available (Exchanges made it mandatory to

promoter and promoter group will be done as per latest available information.
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

7. Action of freezing will not be kept on hold if company is applying for waiver second time after
rejection of first waiver application by Exchange.
8. Unfreezing will be done once company complies and pays fine for all regulations for which

cut-off date, then action for movement to Z/ suspension will be withdrawn.
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

10. The trading in securities of the company will be moved out of Z Category as and when company

11. The Exchanges would continue to apply the jointly decided policy for exemption of fines in

Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

12. Compulsory delisting process shall be initiated within 6 months from the actual date of
suspension, and not from 6 months from the date of completion of weekly trading facility which
is given for six months after the date of actual date of suspension.

documents as per Exchange requirement along with pending Exchange dues within a month
from date of filling application. In case company fails to complete the process with a month then

Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

Detail page: https://www.bseindia.com/static/corporates/non_compliance_new

POLICY FOR EXEMPTION OF FINES LEVIED AS PER THE PROVISIONS OF SEBI SOP CIRCULAR
Reasons for Waiver / Reduction of Penalty levied under SEBI SOP circular
For considering a company's case for waiver of penalty, the company would be required to
disclose to the Exchange, the events that prevent / impact filing of compliances as mentioned in
SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (`Listing Regulations'),
as amended from time to time, either immediately or as soon as practically possible. Further, a
case for waiver or reduction of fine shall be considered only where the applicant company has
fully complied with all its compliances under the Listing Regulations, other applicable regulations
and circulars issued thereunder.
The events referred to below, shall be disclosed along with the relevant supporting documents
evidencing the same, including the impact assessment of the event, duly certified by the
Company Secretary or the Compliance Officer. In case of impact on filing of Financials, the same
shall be certified by the Statutory Auditor of the company.
Non-disclosure of the events preventing / impacting filing of compliances in a timely manner
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

may result in rejection of request for waiver / reduction of fine.
The indicative list of events that may be considered by the Exchange for granting waiver or
reduction of fine levied under SOP for compliance with Listing Regulations are mentioned below
along with criteria to be considered:
1. Natural calamity (Act of GOD)
In the event of Natural calamity, the following will be considered while approving such request:
a. Whether the event had occurred during the period under review or during the period of
filing the compliances
b. Where did the event occur and how it impacted the requisite disclosure from being made
in a time bound manner.
c. Event is notified to the Exchange as soon as possible, along with periodic updates.
d. In order to claim the waiver/reduction of penalty, company will have to adequately
demonstrate that the said Natural Calamity resulted in the company not being able to
comply with the applicable Regulations.
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

2. Seizure / Capture of books / computers etc., by regulatory / statutory authorities
On account of seizure of documents / computer hardware / software, etc., as the case may be,
by regulatory or statutory authorities:
a. The event should have been intimated as a material event at the time of seizure / capture
along with the relevant documentation evidencing the same, including the impact
assessment of the event duly certified by the Company Secretary or the Compliance
Officer e.g. seizure report / panchnama.
b. The seizure / capture should have occurred during the periods under review or
during the period of filing the compliances
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

3. Impossibility of Compliance
In case of any non-compliance arising out of inability of company to comply on account of any
of the following reasons:
a) make any appointment to the Board of Directors / of KMPs due to pending approval for
appointment of Directors / KMP etc., from the Government (Ministry)/ Regulator/ Any
Statutory Authority.
b) any steps taken by Government (Ministry)/ Regulator/ Court /Tribunal/ Any Statutory
Authority, resulting in the non-compliance relating to Board composition e.g. appointment
of a nominee director by relevant authorities, leading to the prevailing compliance becoming
a non-compliance
c) casual vacancy caused on account of resignation/ removal/ death/ disappearance of
directors or KMPs
In such cases, the company has to provide evidence that it has taken adequate steps to
remedy the non-compliance within the stipulated time. Such evidence shall, inter alia,
include proof of communication sent to the approving authority seeking approval for the
appointment / receipt of communication from the authorities appointing a nominee director
that resulted in existing compliance becoming non-compliance. In case of the former, such
communication should have been sent by the company to the relevant authority, prior to
the last due date of compliance. In case of extended delays, companies shall have to submit
proof of follow-up communications as well. Lastly, in case of this carve-out the Exchanges
may jointly (where listed at more than one Exchange) decide to withdraw fines levied earlier
also.
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

4. Court / Regulatory directions that resulted or prevented or exempted the disclosure
required to be made or fines required to be paid.
This would include companies which have obtained BIFR/NCLT order exempting the companies
from paying fines or Companies where the Order of Appointment of Provisional / Official
Liquidator has been issued.
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

5. Material events occurring that are beyond the control of the company
Accidental reasons, including those mentioned in the Listing Regulations, e.g. strikes, lockouts
and other reasons. The event shall be disclosed to the Exchange as per Regulation 30 of Listing
Regulations. The event should have been intimated as a material event either immediately or as
soon as practically possible along with the relevant documentation evidencing the same,
including the impact assessment of the event duly certified by the Company Secretary or the
Compliance Officer.
Further as a general principle, waiver or exemption may be considered even for quarters in
which the event has not occurred, but the impact of the event as mentioned prevents the
company from complying with the disclosures required under the Listing Regulations.
PRE-CONDITIONS FOR ACCEPTING APPLICATIONS FOR FULL / PARTIAL WAIVER OF FINES
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

1. The above list of events may be revised from time to time by the Exchanges after joint
consultation and disseminated on the Exchange websites. The Exchanges may jointly
consider any event which is not mentioned in the above list that deserves full or partial
exemption / waiver based on reasons recorded in writing. However, the governing
principle while considering such exemption / reduction in penalty, shall be that the non-
compliance has occurred due to circumstances which were beyond the control of the
Company and the Company has demonstrated that it has taken sufficient steps at the
earliest to rectify the non-compliance and the Company has made disclosure of such
event to the Exchange at the earliest.
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

2. Companies should file their application in the prescribed mode as mentioned in the
notice of levy of penalty, requesting for waiver of fines along with specific reasons for
claiming the same, within 15 days from the date of Exchange communication intimating
about levy of fines, failing which such application shall be liable for rejection.
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

3. Further the happening of any event listed above does not automatically confer any right
or entitlement to waiver of fine and request for waiver/ reduction in penalty shall be
considered only upon the company applying for the waiver with full underlying facts and
evidences and after ascertaining the facts in the matter. It may be noted that the decision
of the Exchange shall be final and repeated applications for waivers that are declined
earlier, would not be entertained, unless there are any mitigating fresh facts. The
Exchange reserves the right to accede to or deny the request for waiver/ reduction in
penalty, for reasons to be recorded in writing.
Chapter VII PENAL ACTIONS FOR NON-COMPLIANCE

4. An illustrative list of scenarios which cannot be considered to fall within the ambit of
"events" entailing waiver or reduction of fine is given below
i. Company has applied for waiver of fine without specifying any reason for the
delayed compliance.
ii. Company has been unable to find suitable candidate for compliance
officer/Director due to ongoing financial position of company, or lack of
operations or is a loss making company.
iii. Company has been unable to file disclosure due to non-receipt of data from
RTA/Depository.
iv. Non-compliance / Delay in compliance due to non-availability of compliance
officer/resignation of compliance officer or directors or KMPs, beyond the
prescribed time available under law.
v. Company is under process of Corporate Debt Restructuring, declared as NPA by
lenders, etc.
Applications for waiver of fines will be considered only after the applicant company has first
complied with the compliance for which it is seeking full / partial waiver of fines, as required
under the Listing Regulation. Till the time the waiver request is decided by the Exchange, further
penal actions such as freezing of promoter's holdings, shifting to Z category and suspension of
trading in securities may be kept on hold only for those companies whose requests for waivers
fall under the Criteria 1 to 5 given above on Page 1 and 2.
Supreme Court · 2026 INSC 6

Unilaterally appointed sole arbitrators

Is an award by a sole arbitrator appointed by one party alone valid, and can the other party lose its objection by taking part in the arbitration?

['The unilateral appointment of a sole arbitrator is void from the start, and the arbitrator is ineligible under section 12(5) read with the Seventh Schedule. Where the arbitration agreement itself breaches section 12(5), no appointment made under it is valid.', 'Ineligibility can be waived only by an express agreement in writing after disputes arise. It cannot be waived by implication or conduct.', 'An arbitrator who is ineligible lacks inherent jurisdiction, so the objection can be raised at any stage, including for the first time in a challenge to the award under section 34.']

['Recovery awards obtained through a sole arbitrator named by the lender alone can be set aside even if the borrower took part without objecting. Lenders should obtain a clear written waiver after the dispute arises, or have the arbitrator appointed jointly, by an institution or by the court.', 'Lenders and brokers should review loan agreements, client agreements and pending arbitrations for unilateral appointment clauses.']

Statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 12(5), 14, 18, 34 and Seventh Schedule
Supreme Court · 2025 INSC 847

SARFAESI: tenants claiming occupation

Can a person claiming an old, unregistered tenancy get back possession of a mortgaged property that a housing finance company has taken under SARFAESI?

['A person claiming tenancy through an oral or unregistered agreement must prove it with independent evidence such as rent receipts, tax receipts or electricity bills for the period before the demand notice under section 13(2).', 'Even if proved, such a tenancy does not continue beyond one year from the section 13(2) notice; after that the occupant is a tenant at sufferance.', "A recital in the sale deed or a letter of attornment from the borrower is not enough. The High Court's order restoring possession was set aside."]

['Lenders can resist tenancy claims set up to block possession of mortgaged homes, by insisting on proof of occupation before the demand notice.', 'At loan origination, HFCs should record who occupies the property and on what terms.']

Statutes: SARFAESI Act, 2002, ss. 13(2), 13(4), 17(4A); Transfer of Property Act, 1882; West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997
Supreme Court · 2025 INSC 268

Substantial disclosure is enough

Can a life insurer reject a claim because the insured disclosed one large existing policy but not some smaller ones?

['No. The insured had disclosed a Rs 40 lakh policy, much larger than the undisclosed policies and the policy in question. That was a substantial disclosure.', 'The undisclosed policies were of inconsequential amounts, and their omission was not a material suppression. The repudiation was set aside.']

["Not every omission is material. Insurers should ask whether the missing fact would have changed a prudent insurer's decision before repudiating."]

Statutes: Insurance Act, 1938, s. 45; Consumer Protection Act, 1986
Supreme Court · 2025 INSC 174

Broker-client arbitration and family accounts

Can a broker invoke exchange arbitration against a husband for his wife's trading debt, based on an oral arrangement?

["Yes. Courts must read contracts practically, looking at the parties' conduct and intention. The husband's oral instructions and the joint way the two accounts were operated showed joint and several liability.", 'Separate client registration agreements, client codes and accounts did not change this. Arbitration under the exchange bye-laws was maintainable against the husband.']

["Brokers who act on a client's oral instructions to move credit balances to a family member's account may be able to recover from both. This does not relax SEBI's requirements on evidence of client orders, which still apply."]

Statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 7, 34, 37; BSE Bye-laws, 1957
Supreme Court · 2024 INSC 1044

Credit card interest rates

Could the National Consumer Commission cap credit card interest at 30% a year as an unfair trade practice?

["The National Commission's ruling that interest above 30% a year is usurious was set aside. It was contrary to section 21A of the Banking Regulation Act, which bars courts and tribunals from reopening a bank transaction on the ground that the interest is excessive, and it encroached on RBI's domain.", "Directions and guidelines issued by RBI are an extension of the statute. Interest charged as RBI's circulars allow is not an unfair trade practice in itself.", "The complaint was not maintainable: the trusts that filed it were not 'persons' or consumers, and no permission to sue in a representative capacity had been obtained."]

["Interest on credit cards and loans is set by the lender's Board-approved policy within RBI's framework, not by consumer forums. Transparency rules (KFS, APR and disclosure of charges) still apply.", 'The bar in section 21A is written for banking companies, so NBFCs should rely on the RBI framework and fair-dealing rules rather than on section 21A itself.']

Statutes: Banking Regulation Act, 1949, s. 21A; Consumer Protection Act, 1986
Supreme Court (Constitution Bench) · 2024 INSC 857

Unilateral appointment of arbitrators

Is a clause valid if it lets one party appoint a sole arbitrator, or makes the other side choose from a panel curated by that party?

['Equal treatment of parties applies at every stage of arbitration, including the appointment of arbitrators.', "A clause that lets one party unilaterally appoint a sole arbitrator gives rise to justifiable doubts about the arbitrator's independence and impartiality, and hinders the other party's equal participation. For a three-member tribunal, forcing the other party to pick its arbitrator from a panel curated by one side breaches equal treatment.", 'A party can still expressly waive the objection in writing after disputes arise (proviso to section 12(5)). The Court said the law it laid down applies prospectively to appointments made after 8 November 2024, and that this direction applies to three-member tribunals.']

['Loan agreements that let the lender alone name the arbitrator are unsafe. Lenders should agree on the arbitrator with the borrower, use an arbitral institution, or apply to the court under section 11.', 'Awards by an arbitrator the lender appointed alone, without an express written waiver by the borrower after the dispute arose, are at risk of being set aside. Bhadra International (2026) confirms that such a sole arbitrator is ineligible.']

Statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 12(5), 18
Supreme Court · 2024 INSC 296

Insurer's burden to prove suppression

Who must prove that the insured suppressed other policies, and with what evidence?

['Where the insurer repudiates on the ground of suppression, the burden is on the insurer to prove that the fact suppressed was material and that the insured knew of it.', 'The insurer had produced no documents to show the other policies. The repudiation could not stand.']

["Claims teams must keep documentary proof, such as other insurers' records, before repudiating for non-disclosure. Allegations alone will fail."]

Statutes: Insurance Act, 1938, s. 45 (before the 2015 amendment); Evidence Act, 1872
Supreme Court · 2023 INSC 1076

Nominee versus legal heirs

Does a nominee of shares or securities become the owner on the holder's death, to the exclusion of the legal heirs?

['No. The nominee does not get absolute title. Vesting in the nominee under section 109A of the Companies Act, 1956 (section 72 of the 2013 Act) and Bye-law 9.11.1 under the Depositories Act is for a limited purpose.', 'Nomination does not change the law of succession. The legal heirs, or the beneficiaries under a will, remain entitled.']

['Depository participants, brokers and registrars can transmit securities to the nominee to complete formalities, but the nominee holds them subject to the claims of the legal heirs.', 'Client communication should say clearly that a nomination is not a will.']

Statutes: Companies Act, 2013, s. 72; Companies Act, 1956, ss. 109A, 109B; Depositories Act, 1996 and depository bye-laws
Supreme Court · 2023 INSC 1018

Insolvency of personal guarantors

Are sections 95 to 100 of the IBC, on insolvency of individuals such as personal guarantors, constitutional?

['Sections 95 to 100 are valid and do not violate Articles 14 and 21.', 'The resolution professional only facilitates and recommends. No adjudication happens until the Adjudicating Authority decides under section 100, and natural justice must be observed at that stage.', 'No hearing is needed before the resolution professional is appointed under section 97(5). The debtor can take part when the resolution professional examines the application under section 99. The interim moratorium under section 96 stays legal proceedings in respect of any debt.']

["Lenders can file insolvency against personal guarantors of corporate borrowers without a prior hearing on 'jurisdictional facts'. The guarantor is heard in the resolution professional's examination and before the Adjudicating Authority decides."]

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 95-100
Supreme Court · 2023 INSC 838

SARFAESI: right of redemption

Until when can a borrower redeem a mortgaged property that a secured creditor is selling under SARFAESI?

["Under section 13(8) of SARFAESI as amended in 2016, the borrower's right to redeem ends on the date the auction notice is published under Rule 9(1) of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, not when the sale is completed.", 'SARFAESI, as a special law with an overriding clause, prevails over the general right of redemption in section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act.', 'Once the sale is confirmed, the lender cannot withhold the sale certificate and make a private settlement with the borrower. High Courts should not use writ jurisdiction to undo an auction when the remedy under section 17 is available.']

['Borrowers must pay in full before the auction notice is published. After that, lenders should complete the sale and should not accept late settlements that defeat the auction purchaser.', 'Auction purchasers get firmer title, which supports bids at SARFAESI auctions.']

Statutes: SARFAESI Act, 2002, ss. 13(8), 17; Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002, r. 9; Transfer of Property Act, 1882, s. 60
Supreme Court · 2023 INSC 379

SARFAESI: writs against lenders

Should High Courts entertain writ petitions against SARFAESI notices when the Debts Recovery Tribunal is available?

['The power under Article 226 is wide but should be used only in extraordinary cases. Where the legislature has provided a specific remedy, as SARFAESI does through the Debts Recovery Tribunal, the writ remedy should not be used.', 'A writ of mandamus in a commercial matter against a private party needs a clear legal right, and more caution is needed when the respondent is a private lender.']

['Borrowers challenging SARFAESI measures will normally be sent to the DRT under section 17. This reduces stays obtained through writ petitions.']

Statutes: SARFAESI Act, 2002, ss. 13(4), 17; Constitution of India, Art. 226
Supreme Court · 2023 INSC 303

Fraud classification

Must a lender hear the borrower before classifying its account as fraud under RBI's Master Directions on Frauds?

["Classifying an account as fraud has civil consequences for the borrower: the penal measures that apply to wilful defaulters, no restructuring and, in effect, a credit freeze that the Court described as close to 'civil death'.", 'The Master Directions do not expressly exclude a hearing, so the rule of audi alteram partem is read into them. The borrower must be given notice, a chance to explain the forensic audit findings and to make a representation before the account is classified as fraud.', 'The decision classifying the account as fraud must be made by a reasoned order.']

['Every fraud classification needs a show-cause notice with the material relied on, a real chance to reply in writing, and a reasoned order. Classifications made without these are open to challenge in writ proceedings.', 'In State Bank of India v. Amit Iron Pvt Ltd (7 April 2026, 2026 INSC 323) the Supreme Court held that the borrower has no right to a personal hearing, and that forensic audit reports the lender relies on should be furnished to the borrower. A lender that wants to withhold a report to protect third parties must first show that disclosure would affect their rights.', "RBI's Fraud Risk Management Directions for NBFCs now build these steps into the process."]

Statutes: RBI Act, 1934; Banking Regulation Act, 1949; RBI Master Directions on Frauds, 2016
Supreme Court · 2022 INSC 829

Distributor commission on winding up

Are mutual fund distributors entitled to trail commission from a scheme that is being wound up?

['Regulation 52, which allows recurring expenses including distributor commission, applies only while a scheme is operating, not after the notice of winding up is published.', "Distributor commission is not an expense connected with winding up. Future trail commission is not an amount 'due and payable' at the time of winding up."]

['Once a winding-up notice is published, distributors stop earning trail commission from that scheme. The SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 now say expressly that distribution commission is not a winding-up cost (regulation 38(1)(d), Explanation).']

Statutes: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, regs. 39-41, 52; SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026, reg. 38
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 853

Changed terms on renewal

Can a health insurer rely on a new cap on cover that it introduced at renewal without telling the policyholder?

['The policyholders were led to believe they were renewing the same policy, while the insurer had introduced caps on certain surgical procedures. The insurer had a duty to tell them about the new limits.', "Failing to disclose the changed terms was a deficiency in service. The District Forum's order allowing the claim was restored."]

['Any change to cover at renewal, particularly limits and sub-limits, must be clearly told to the policyholder before renewal. Otherwise the insurer may be held to the earlier terms.']

Statutes: Consumer Protection Act, 1986, s. 2(1)(g); IRDAI (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 826

Pre-existing conditions disclosed at proposal

Can a health insurer reject a claim by citing a medical condition that the insured disclosed, and that the insurer assessed, before issuing the policy?

['The insurer must assess the risks from the health condition disclosed in the proposal form before it issues the policy.', 'Once the policy is issued after that assessment, the insurer cannot reject a claim by citing a disclosed existing condition that led to the risk claimed for.']

['Underwriting must be done before issue. A health insurer that conducted a medical examination and accepted disclosed conditions cannot later rely on them to repudiate.']

Statutes: Consumer Protection Act, 1986; Indian Contract Act, 1872 (utmost good faith)
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 333

Winding up: trustees and SEBI powers

Can trustees wind up a scheme without unitholders' prior consent, and are Regulations 39 to 42 valid?

['Regulations 39 to 42 are valid. Being economic regulations, they get judicial restraint.', "Read together with Regulation 18(15)(c), the trustees' opinion that the scheme should be wound up stands, but the consent of unitholders is a precondition for the winding up."]

['Trustees cannot close a scheme on their own. They need unitholder consent, which shapes how stress in debt schemes is handled. Under regulation 36(5) of the 2026 Regulations, a scheme reopens for business if consent is not obtained.']

Statutes: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, regs. 18(15)(c), 39-42; SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026, regs. 36-38; SEBI Act, 1992
Delhi High Court · W.P.(C) 3190/2021

Cover for mental illness

Can a health insurer treat mental illness differently from physical illness?

['Section 21(4) of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 requires every insurer to provide medical insurance for treatment of mental illness on the same basis as physical illness. Insurers are bound by the Act regardless of any circular.', 'The insurer was ordered to pay costs because the policyholder had to litigate. IRDAI was asked to ensure that all insurers give effect to section 21(4) from 29 May 2018, when it came into force.']

['Health policies cannot exclude or sub-limit mental illness in a way that does not apply to physical illness. Claims for mental health treatment must be assessed on the same basis.']

Statutes: Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, s. 21(4)
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 203

COVID-19 moratorium and interest

Could courts order a full interest waiver, sector-wise relief or a longer moratorium during the COVID-19 pandemic?

['Economic and financial policy of RBI and the Government is open to only limited judicial review. Courts will not order particular relief packages, a full waiver of interest or a longer moratorium.', 'No interest on interest, compound interest or penal interest could be charged for the moratorium period. Any amount already recovered had to be refunded or adjusted in the next instalment.']

['Lenders had to reverse interest on interest and penal interest for the moratorium period for all borrowers.', 'Courts will usually defer to RBI on the design of relief and restructuring schemes, unless they are arbitrary, mala fide or contrary to law.']

Statutes: Disaster Management Act, 2005; RBI COVID-19 Regulatory Package circulars, 2020
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 87

Winding up: unitholders' consent

When trustees wind up a scheme, what does 'consent of the unitholders' under Regulation 18(15)(c) mean?

['Consent means consent of a majority of the unitholders who take part in the poll, not a majority of all unitholders of the scheme.', 'Consent of the majority binds all unitholders, including those who did not agree. The Court accepted the e-voting results for the six schemes.']

["Trustees seeking unitholders' consent to wind up need a simple majority of those voting. Regulation 36(4) of the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 now writes this in: votes are counted at one vote per unit, and results must be published within 45 calendar days of the winding-up notice."]

Statutes: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, regs. 18(15)(c), 39
Supreme Court · 2021 INSC 28

Minimum number of homebuyers to file

Is the 2020 amendment requiring at least 100 allottees, or 10% of allottees, of the same project (whichever is less) to file an insolvency application valid?

['The threshold is valid. A critical mass of allottees of the same real estate project must agree before the Code is triggered.', 'Allottees are financial creditors, but they have features that set them apart from other financial creditors, such as their large numbers, which justify the separate threshold.']

['An individual homebuyer can no longer push a developer into insolvency unless the threshold is met, which in a small project may need only a few allottees. Housing finance lenders to developers face fewer stray insolvency filings, though collective filings remain possible.']

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2020, s. 3; Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, s. 7(1)
Supreme Court · 2020 INSC 264

Limits of RBI's powers

Could RBI direct the entities it regulates to stop serving anyone dealing in virtual currencies?

['The RBI Act, the Banking Regulation Act and the Payment and Settlement Systems Act together give RBI very wide powers over the currency, credit and payment systems, enough to cover virtual currency activity that may affect them.', 'However, the circular of 6 April 2018 failed the test of proportionality, because RBI had not found that virtual currency exchanges had actually harmed the entities it regulates. The circular was set aside.']

["RBI's directions to regulated entities are tested for proportionality as well as for power. A blanket ban needs evidence of harm and a look at less drastic options.", "The judgment confirms how wide RBI's statutory powers are, including the NBFC powers in Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act."]

Statutes: RBI Act, 1934, ss. 45JA, 45L; Banking Regulation Act, 1949, ss. 35A, 36; Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007
Supreme Court · 2019 INSC 1067

SARFAESI: who can order possession

Can a Chief Judicial Magistrate deal with a secured creditor's request under section 14 of SARFAESI to take possession?

['Yes. In non-metropolitan areas the Chief Judicial Magistrate is competent, as the expressions CMM and CJM are interchangeable. This settled conflicting High Court views.', "The power under section 14 is non-judicial: it is the State's coercive power to help the secured creditor take possession."]

['Lenders outside metropolitan areas can apply to the CJM as well as the District Magistrate under section 14, which helps when the DM is slow to act.']

Statutes: SARFAESI Act, 2002, s. 14; Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
Supreme Court · 2019 INSC 889

Homebuyers as financial creditors

Is the 2018 amendment to the IBC that treats allottees of real estate projects as financial creditors constitutional?

['The amendment is valid. Allottees are financial creditors who can start insolvency under section 7 and sit on the Committee of Creditors through authorised representatives.', 'RERA must be read harmoniously with the Code. Where the two conflict, the Code prevails.']

["In a builder's insolvency, homebuyers can hold a large share of the votes in the Committee of Creditors. Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 5(8)(f), 21(6A), 25A; Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016
Supreme Court · 2019 INSC 652

Wilful defaulters

Can a borrower be represented by a lawyer before a lender's committees that decide wilful default?

["The in-house committees under RBI's wilful defaulter circular exercise administrative, not judicial, power. A borrower has no right to be represented by a lawyer before them.", "Being declared a wilful defaulter directly affects the right to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g). ['Wilful default classification needs a show-cause notice, a chance to reply, a reasoned order and review. Under the judgment, lawyers can be kept out of the in-house proceedings.', "RBI's Wilful Defaulter Directions of 2024 now go further: the Review Committee must also give the borrower, guarantor, promoter or director an opportunity for a personal hearing. Statutes: Advocates Act, 1961, s. 30; Constitution of India, Art. 19(1)(g); RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters, 2015
Supreme Court · 2019 INSC 565

Disclosure of other policies

Can a life insurer repudiate because the insured did not disclose another life policy taken shortly before?

['Insurance contracts rest on utmost good faith. The duty of full disclosure means no information of substance or interest to the insurer may be omitted or concealed.', "The insured had answered 'no' when asked about existing cover, two months after taking another policy. The repudiation was within the period allowed by section 45 and was upheld."]

['Questions on existing cover in the proposal form are material. Insurers can rely on wrong answers to them, within the time allowed by section 45.', 'Section 45 was amended in 2015: a life policy now cannot be questioned on any ground after three years from the date of issue, commencement of risk, revival or rider, whichever is later. Statutes: Insurance Act, 1938, s. 45; Consumer Protection Act, 1986
Supreme Court · 2019 INSC 457

RBI powers over stressed assets

Was RBI's circular of 12 February 2018 on resolution of stressed assets (the 'one-day default' framework) within its powers?

['Sections 35AA and 35AB of the Banking Regulation Act are valid. ["RBI's power to push lenders into insolvency is case-specific. Statutes: Banking Regulation Act, 1949, ss. 21, 35A, 35AA, 35AB; RBI Act, 1934, s. 45L; Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
Supreme Court · 2019 INSC 95

Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code upheld

Is the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code constitutional, in particular its different treatment of financial and operational creditors?

['The Code is constitutionally valid.', 'Financial creditors are different from operational creditors: they are best placed to assess the viability of the corporate debtor and the resolution plan. ['Financial creditors, including NBFCs and HFCs, vote in the Committee of Creditors and so have a strong say in the outcome. Section 7 is a route to collective resolution of a defaulting company, not a debt collection tool, though lenders often recover through it.']

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
Supreme Court · 2018 INSC 119

Can pre-arranged, reversed trades in the futures and options segment be manipulative, even though they are cash-settled?

['Yes. Trading is meant to make profit. Where one party consistently loses in pre-planned, rapid reversal trades, the trades are not genuine and amount to an unfair trade practice.', 'The Securities Appellate Tribunal was wrong to hold that such trades in the F&O segment cannot manipulate the market because there is no change of beneficial ownership.', "SEBI's appeals against the brokers were dismissed. ['Clients who trade in pre-arranged reversals in derivatives are exposed to action even though the trades are cash-settled. A broker is liable only on proof of its own negligence or connivance, so surveillance alerts and records of client instructions matter.']

Statutes: SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations, 2003, regs. 3, 4; SEBI (Stock Brokers) Regulations
Supreme Court · 2017 INSC 963

Front-running

Can front-running by persons who are not intermediaries be punished under the PFUTP Regulations?

["Information about trades a large investor is about to place is that investor's confidential information.", "A person who passes on such information in breach of duty, and a 'tippee' who knows of the breach and trades on it, can both be liable for fraud under Regulations 3 and 4(1) of the PFUTP Regulations. ["Fund managers, dealers and anyone with advance knowledge of a fund's orders, and those they tip off, are exposed to SEBI action. AMCs need controls on order information and on staff and related-party trading."]

Statutes: SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to Securities Market) Regulations, 2003, regs. 3, 4(1); SEBI Act, 1992
Supreme Court · 2016 INSC 201

Proof of manipulation by brokers

What proof does SEBI need to hold a broker or sub-broker liable for manipulative trading?

["Brokers can be penalised on circumstantial evidence for trades placed for clients, especially in illiquid scrips. Know-your-client checks, surveillance alerts and records of client instructions are the broker's main defence."]

Statutes: SEBI Act, 1992; SEBI (Stock Brokers and Sub-Brokers) Regulations, 1992; SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations, 2003
Supreme Court · 2015 INSC 946

Assignment of life policies

Could an insurer refuse to register assignments of life policies made for trading?

Statutes: Insurance Act, 1938, s. 38
Supreme Court · 2015 INSC 942

RBI inspection reports under RTI

Can RBI refuse to disclose inspection reports and other information about the entities it regulates under the Right to Information Act?

['RBI does not hold such information in a fiduciary relationship with the banks it regulates, and cannot refuse disclosure on the grounds of economic interest or commercial confidence in this case.', "Inspection reports and similar documents obtained by RBI from a regulated entity are 'information' under section 2(f) of the RTI Act. ['Findings in RBI inspection reports can become public through RTI requests, subject to the exemptions in section 8 that apply on the facts. Regulated entities should expect supervisory findings to be disclosable.']

Supreme Court · 2014 INSC 678

Exchange's lien over a defaulting broker

When a broker defaults, who gets paid first from the membership card and the deposited securities: the stock exchange or the Income Tax Department?

["Securities a broker has deposited with the exchange are first applied to the broker's obligations under the exchange's rules, ahead of tax dues. The membership card's value is not available to the tax department."]

Statutes: Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and Rules; Income Tax Act, 1961, s. 226(3)
Supreme Court · 2011 INSC 793

Repossession by force

Can a financier take back a vehicle by force under a hire-purchase agreement?

['Even for goods under hire-purchase, recovery must follow the law. The owner-financier cannot use force to take back possession on the strength of the agreement.', "RBI's guidelines support this. ['Vehicle and asset financiers must repossess through lawful process, with no force or intimidation. Recovery agents act for the lender, and the lender answers for them.', 'Consumer forums can award compensation for unlawful repossession.']

Statutes: Consumer Protection Act, 1986; RBI Fair Practices Code and recovery guidelines
